Playwright Test supports a timeout for the whole test run. This prevents excess resource usage when everything went wrong. There is no default global timeout, but you can set a reasonable one in the config, for example one hour. Global timeout produces the following error:

reference: Web-first assertions retry for about 5 seconds by default, and that clock runs independently of the overall test timeout.
reference_contexts: Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout. It produces the following error:
llm_response: By default, web-first assertions like `toHaveText` have a timeout of 5 seconds.
llm_references:
`expect`
now supports lots of new web-first assertions.

Consider the following example:


`awaitexpect(page.locator('.status')).toHaveText('Submitted');`


Playwright Test will be re-testing the node with the selector
`.status`
until fetched Node has the
`"Submitted"`
text. It will be re-fetching the node and checking it over and over, until the condition is met or until the timeout is reached. You can either pass this timeout or configure it once via the
testProject.expect (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-expect)
value in test config.

By default, the timeout for assertions is not set, so it'll wait forever, until the whole test times out.

List of all new assertions:

`awaitexpect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');`


Playwright will be re-testing the element with the test id of
`status`
until the fetched element has the
`"Submitted"`
text. It will re-fetch the element and check it over and over, until the condition is met or until the timeout is reached. You can either pass this timeout or configure it once via the
testConfig.expect (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-expect)
value in the test config.

By default, the timeout for assertions is set to 5 seconds. Learn more about
various timeouts (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-timeouts)
.

## Auto-retrying assertions​ {#auto-retrying-assertions}

The following assertions will retry until the assertion passes, or the assertion timeout is reached. Note that retrying assertions are async, so you must
`await`
them.

## Non-retrying assertions​ {#non-retrying-assertions}

These assertions allow to test any conditions, but do not auto-retry. Most of the time, web pages show information asynchronously, and using non-retrying assertions can lead to a flaky test.

Prefer
auto-retrying (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions#auto-retrying-assertions)
assertions whenever possible. For more complex assertions that need to be retried, use
expect.poll (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions#expectpoll)
or
expect.toPass (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-assertions#expecttopass)
.

user_input: I have a flaky test I'd like re-run a couple of times on failure — what's the quickest command-line way?
reference: Pass a retry count on the run command, e.g. npx playwright test --retries=3 re-runs failing tests up to three times. Nothing is retried unless you opt in.
reference_contexts: Playwright supports test retries . When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.
llm_response:
The quickest command-line way to re-run flaky tests is to use the `--retries` flag. You can specify the number of retry attempts as follows:

`npx playwright test --retries=<number>`

For example, to give failing tests 3 retry attempts, use:
`npx playwright test --retries=3`

Playwright Test will categorize tests as follows:

# Retries | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Test retries are a way to automatically re-run a test when it fails. This is useful when a test is flaky and fails intermittently. Test retries are configured in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

## Failures​ {#failures}

Playwright Test runs tests in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

Consider the following snippet:


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe('suite',()=>{test.beforeAll(async()=>{/* ... */});test('first good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('second flaky',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('third good',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test.afterAll(async()=>{/* ... */});});`


When
all tests pass
, they will run in order in the same worker process.

user_input: Do I get videos of my test runs automatically, or do I have to switch them on?
reference: They stay off unless you opt in; a single config setting — video — turns recording on and selects the mode.

llm_response:
You have to switch them on. By default, video recording is turned off.

To enable it, you must set the `video` option in your `playwright.config.ts` (or `playwright.config.js`) file. The available options are:

*   `'on'`: Record video for each test.
*   `'retain-on-failure'`: Record video for each test, but remove all videos from successful test runs.
*   `'on-first-retry'`: Record video only when retrying a test for the first time.
*   `'off'`: Do not record video (default).

## Properly handling Secrets​ {#properly-handling-secrets}

Artifacts like trace files, HTML reports or even the console logs contain information about your test execution. They can contain sensitive data like user credentials for a test user, access tokens to a staging backend, testing source code, or sometimes even your application source code. Treat these files just as carefully as you treat that sensitive data. If you upload reports and traces as part of your CI workflow, make sure that you only upload them to trusted artifact stores, or that you encrypt the files before upload. The same is true for sharing artifacts with team members: Use a trusted file share or encrypt the files before sharing.

user_input: How can I cap how many tests run in parallel straight from the command line?
reference: Bound the parallel worker count with the --workers flag, e.g. npx playwright test --workers 4.
reference_contexts: npx playwright test --workers 4
llm_response:
To cap the number of tests running in parallel, you can use the `--workers` command line flag. You can specify the number of concurrent workers or a percentage of logical CPU cores.

You can use either of the following formats:

*   `npx playwright test --workers=<number>`
*   `npx playwright test -j <number>`

For example, to run tests in a single worker (disabling parallelism), you would use:
`npx playwright test --workers=1`

## Shard tests between multiple machines​ {#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines}

Playwright Test can shard a test suite, so that it can be executed on multiple machines. See
sharding guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding)
for more details.


`npx playwrighttest--shard=2/3`


## Limit failures and fail fast​ {#limit-failures-and-fail-fast}

You can limit the number of failed tests in the whole test suite by setting
`maxFailures`
config option or passing
`--max-failures`
command line flag.

When running with "max failures" set, Playwright Test will stop after reaching this number of failed tests and skip any tests that were not executed yet. This is useful to avoid wasting resources on broken test suites.

Passing command line option:


`npx playwrighttest--max-failures=10`

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

By default, tests in a single file are run in order. If you have many independent tests in a single file, you might want to run them in parallel with

reference_contexts: Selects one or multiple options in the <select> element with locator.selectOption() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-select-option) . You can specify option value , or label to select. Multiple options can be selected.
llm_response:
To choose an option in a `<select>` element, use the `selectOption` method. You can select multiple options at once by passing an array of values to the method.

### How to choose options
You can select options by matching their value or label. Examples include:

*   **Single selection by value or label:**
    `await page.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption('blue');`
*   **Single selection by label specifically:**
    `await page.getByLabel('Choose a color').selectOption({ label: 'Blue' });`
*   **Multiple selection:**
    Pass an array of strings to select multiple items:
    `await page.getByLabel('Choose multiple colors').selectOption(['red', 'green', 'blue']);`

### Behavior and Constraints
*   **Multiple selection:** If the `<select>` element has the `multiple` attribute, all matching options provided in the array will be selected. If the `multiple` attribute is not present, only the first option matching one of the passed options will be selected.
*   **Validation:** The method performs actionability checks and waits until all specified options are present in the element. If the target element is not a `<select>` element, the method throws an error.
*   **Events:** The method triggers `change` and `input` events once the options have been selected.
*   **Return value:** It returns an array of the option values that were successfully selected.

Yes, your test will stall. Dialogs are modals that block further page execution until they are handled. If you do not handle the dialog using a `page.on('dialog')` listener, your action (such as `locator.click()`) will stall.

user_input: Where should I keep saved login state, and how do I keep it out of version control?
reference: Stash it in a playwright/.auth directory and add that folder to .gitignore; tests then reuse the saved state to start already signed in.
reference_contexts: We recommend to create playwright/.auth directory and add it to your .gitignore . Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this playwright/.auth directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.
llm_response:
You should save your login state (storage state) to a file, such as `auth.json` or a file within a `playwright/.auth` directory.

To keep this sensitive information out of version control, you must add the file or directory to your `.gitignore` file. The documentation provides the following commands to handle this:

*   **Bash:**
    `mkdir -p playwright/.auth`
    `echo $'\nplaywright/.auth' >> .gitignore`

*   **PowerShell:**
    `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path playwright\.auth`
    `Add-Content -Path .gitignore "`r`nplaywright/.auth"`

*   **Batch:**
    `md playwright\.auth`
    `echo. >> .gitignore`
    `echo "playwright/.auth" >> .gitignore`

The documentation strongly discourages checking these files into private or public repositories because they may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account.

user_input: How do I split my tests to run across several machines at once?
reference: Shard with --shard=x/y — run 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 on four machines so each takes a quarter of the suite.
reference_contexts:
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4

llm_response:
To split your tests to run across several machines at once, you should use the sharding feature. You can shard your test suite by passing the `--shard=x/y` flag to the command line, where `x` is the current shard index and `y` is the total number of shards.

For example, to split your suite into four shards, you would run the following commands on your different machines or CI jobs:

```bash
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4
```

Running these shards in parallel on different jobs allows your test suite to complete faster by utilizing the hardware resources of each machine.

`npx playwrighttest--workers=1`


## Parallelize tests in a single file​ {#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file}

By default, tests in a single file are run in order. If you have many independent tests in a single file, you might want to run them in parallel with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

Note that parallel tests are executed in separate worker processes and cannot share any state or global variables. Each test executes all relevant hooks just for itself, including
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
.


`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test.describe.configure({mode:'parallel'});test('runs in parallel 1',async({page})=>{/* ... */});test('runs in parallel 2',async({page})=>{/* ... */});`


Alternatively, you can opt-in all tests into this fully-parallel mode in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({fullyParallel:true,});`

`test.describe('runs in parallel with other describes',()=>{test.describe.configure({mode:'default'});test('in order 1',async({page})=>{});test('in order 2',async({page})=>{});});`


## Shard tests between multiple machines​ {#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines}

Playwright Test can shard a test suite, so that it can be executed on multiple machines. See
sharding guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-sharding)
for more details.


`npx playwrighttest--shard=2/3`


## Limit failures and fail fast​ {#limit-failures-and-fail-fast}

You can limit the number of failed tests in the whole test suite by setting
`maxFailures`
config option or passing
`--max-failures`
command line flag.

When running with "max failures" set, Playwright Test will stop after reaching this number of failed tests and skip any tests that were not executed yet. This is useful to avoid wasting resources on broken test suites.

Passing command line option:


`npx playwrighttest--max-failures=10`

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

## Sharding tests between multiple machines​ {#sharding-tests-between-multiple-machines}

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:


`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`


Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Similarly, use
`globalTeardown`

reference: Call test.slow() inside it; that marks the test slow and triples its timeout.

## Fixture timeout​ {#fixture-timeout}

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.


`import{testasbase,expect}from'@playwright/test';consttest=base.extend<{slowFixture:string}>({slowFixture:[async({},use)=>{// ... perform a slow operation ...awaituse('hello');},{timeout:60000}]});test('example test',async({slowFixture})=>{// ...});`


Unlike regular test-scoped fixtures, each
worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures)
fixture has its own timeout, equal to the test timeout. You can change the timeout for a worker-scoped fixture in the same way.

`afterAll`

user_input: How do I watch the browser as my script runs and slow it down enough to follow along?
reference: Launch non-headless and pace each step with slowMo — e.g. chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 }).
reference_contexts:
// Chromium, Firefox, or WebKit

llm_response:
To watch your script run in a browser and slow it down to follow along, use the following approaches:

**1. To watch the browser:**
*   **For general scripts:** Use the `headless: false` launch option. For example:
    `await chromium.launch({ headless: false });`
*   **For tests:** Use the Playwright sidebar and enable the **Show Browser** option.

**2. To slow down execution:**
*   **Use the `slowMo` option:** This slows down execution by a specified number of milliseconds per operation. You can combine this with headed mode:
    `await chromium.launch({ headless: false, slowMo: 100 });`

**Note on `test.slow()`:**
Do not use `test.slow()` to slow down the execution speed of your script. According to the documentation, `test.slow()` is used to mark a test as "slow" to give it triple the default timeout, rather than to introduce a delay between operations.

user_input: My e2e tests mutate shared server state and run in parallel. What auth model avoids collisions, and how do workers stay on separate accounts?
reference: Give each parallel worker its own account and authenticate it once with a worker-scoped fixture. Key the account on the worker's parallelIndex — which stays the same even when a worker restarts — so a worker always maps to the same account.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state . In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between 0 and workers - 1 . When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same parallelIndex and a new workerIndex .
llm_response:
To avoid collisions when e2e tests mutate shared server state in parallel, the recommended approach is to use the **"one account per parallel worker"** model.

### How to stay on separate accounts
To implement this, you must ensure each parallel worker is authenticated with a unique account:

*   **Authenticate per worker:** You must authenticate once per worker process, assigning each a unique account.
*   **Use a worker fixture:** Create a `playwright/fixtures.ts` file to override the `storageState` fixture. This allows you to authenticate once per worker.
*   **Differentiate workers:** Use `testInfo.parallelIndex` within your fixture to differentiate between the workers.
*   **Acquire unique accounts:** You can either acquire a unique account dynamically (e.g., `const account = await acquireAccount(id)`) or use a list of pre-created accounts. Ensure these accounts are unique so that multiple workers (or team members) can run tests simultaneously without interference. 

Once authenticated, the worker process reuses that specific authentication state for all tests it runs.

## Moderate: one account per parallel worker​ {#moderate-one-account-per-parallel-worker}

This is the
recommended
approach for tests that
modify server-side state
. In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

When to use

### Implementation Steps

1.  **Create an authentication setup file:** Create a file (e.g., `tests/auth.setup.ts`) to perform the authentication steps. In this file, navigate to your login page, perform the sign-in actions, and ensure the cookies are set (e.g., by waiting for a specific URL or element).

reference_contexts: When fullyParallel: true is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. ### Balancing Shards
*   **`fullyParallel: true` (Recommended):** This enables test-level granularity. Playwright distributes individual tests across shards, which is the preferred method for ensuring an even load distribution.
*   **Without `fullyParallel`:** Playwright defaults to file-level granularity. Shards are assigned entire test files. To maintain balance in this mode, you must manually ensure your test files are small and evenly sized; otherwise, some shards may run significantly more tests than others.

### Workers and Parallelism
*   Sharding allows you to split your test suite into multiple parts (e.g., `--shard=x/y`) to run them simultaneously across different CI jobs.
*   Each shard utilizes available CPU cores to run tests in parallel. Playwright can only shard tests that are capable of being run in parallel.

### Retries
*   You can use the `--retries` flag to set a maximum retry count for flaky tests.
*   When using retries, you can configure tracing modes (e.g., `on-first-retry`, `on-all-retries`, or `retain-on-failure-and-retries`) to assist in debugging reliability issues.

Project dependencies are preferred because they integrate better with the Playwright test runner compared to the `globalSetup` config option. Specifically, project dependencies provide the following advantages:

*   **Reporting:** Global setup actions are shown in the HTML report as a separate project.
*   **Artifacts:** Full trace recording is supported and available.
*   **Fixtures:** Playwright fixtures are fully supported.
*   **Browser Management:** You can use the `browser` fixture rather than manual browser launching.
*   **Configuration:** Config options like `headless` or `testIdAttribute` are automatically applied.
*   **Parallelism:** Supported via standard configuration.

In contrast, the `globalSetup` config option lacks support for traces, fixtures, and automatic application of config options, and it is not shown in the HTML report. You should consider using project dependencies to ensure full feature support.

## Option 1: Project Dependencies​ {#option-1-project-dependencies}

Project dependencies (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-dependencies)
are a list of projects that need to run before the tests in another project run. They can be useful for configuring the global setup actions so that one project depends on this running first. Using dependencies allows global setup to produce traces and other artifacts.

### Setup​ {#setup}

To learn more, see our
Project Dependencies guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-projects)
.

### Global Setup​ {#global-setup}

For tasks that need to run only once before all tests (like seeding a database), use
Global Setup
. You can trigger the global setup and teardown manually from the Playwright sidebar.

### Multiple Configurations​ {#multiple-configurations}

If you have multiple
`playwright.config.ts`
files, you can switch between them using the gear icon in the Playwright sidebar. This allows you to easily work with different test suites or environments.

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

There are two ways to configure global setup and teardown: using a global setup file and setting it in the config under
globalSetup (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-global-setup-teardown#option-2-configure-globalsetup-and-globalteardown)
or using
project dependencies (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-global-setup-teardown#option-1-project-dependencies)
. With project dependencies, you define a project that runs before all other projects. This is the recommended approach, as it integrates better with the Playwright test runner: your HTML report will include the global setup, traces will be recorded, and fixtures can be used. For a detailed comparison of the two approaches, see the table below.

user_input: Our app registers a service worker for offline support. Every route handler I install works fine against a build with the worker disabled, but against the real build some requests reach the network untouched while others are intercepted, and which is which seems to change between runs. What decides whether a request is interceptable here, and what's the sane way to test against this app?
reference: Whether a request is routable depends on who owns it. Once a service worker with a fetch handler is installed it sits between the page and the network: the page-owned request is served by the worker and never reaches the network, so it isn't routable, while the worker's own outbound request is a separate, service-worker-owned request that context routing does see. That split is why interception looks inconsistent — you're catching some requests at one layer and missing others at the other, and which layer serves a given resource depends on the worker's cache state, hence the run-to-run variation. If you're doing ordinary network mocking, the documented answer is not to reason about this at all: set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the config's `use` options so the worker never registers and everything is page-owned and routable. Only if you specifically need to assert on the worker's own traffic should you leave them enabled and branch inside the handler on `route.request().serviceWorker()` — noting that calling .frame() on such a request throws, and that requests for updated worker scripts cannot currently be routed at all.

Playwright provides built-in APIs for this use case that don't require the information below. However, if you're interested in requests made by Service Workers themselves, please read below.

llm_response:
Whether a request is interceptable depends on whether it is handled by a Service Worker's fetch handler. Requests intercepted by a Service Worker will not be intercepted by `page.route()` or `browserContext.route()`. Because Service Workers act as a network proxy, they can prevent requests from reaching the external network, making them non-routable via Playwright's interception methods. The inconsistent behavior you observe occurs because requests handled by a Service Worker's fetch handler return `true` for `response.fromServiceWorker()`, while others may not.

The recommended way to test against an app that uses Service Workers when you need to use request interception is to disable the Service Workers entirely. You can do this by setting `serviceWorkers` to `'block'` in your browser context options:

*   **In `browser.newContext()`:**
    ```javascript
    const context = await browser.newContext({ serviceWorkers: 'block' });
    ```
*   **In `playwright.config.ts`:**
    Set `testOptions.serviceWorkers` to `'block'`.

Disabling them makes tests more predictable and ensures that your route handlers function consistently.

user_input: Our GitHub Actions job installs cleanly — `npm ci` is green — and then every test fails at browser launch complaining about missing shared libraries. It's an ubuntu-latest runner, and the identical commit runs fine on all three of our developers' machines. What is the CI box missing that a laptop already has, and what's the durable way to fix it?
reference: Installing the npm package is not the same as provisioning a machine that can run browsers, and that's the gap. `npm ci` fetches the library; the browser binaries are downloaded separately, and those binaries need operating-system level libraries that a developer machine already has from everyday browser use and a bare Linux runner does not. So there are two things to install, and the combined step is `npx playwright install --with-deps`, which fetches the browsers and the OS dependencies together — that's exactly the step the recommended GitHub Actions workflow runs between `npm ci` and the test command. The alternative, and the more durable one if you also do visual comparison, is to run the job inside the official container image via `jobs.<job_id>.container`: it keeps the dependencies out of the host environment and gives you a consistent rendering environment, which matters because screenshots differ across platforms.
reference_contexts: Ensure CI agent can run browsers: Use our Docker image in Linux agents or install your dependencies using the CLI.
# Install NPM packages npm ci # Install Playwright browsers and dependencies npx playwright install --with-deps
The Command line tools can be used to install all operating system dependencies in CI.

GitHub Actions support running jobs in a container by using the jobs.<job_id>.container option. This is useful to not pollute the host environment with dependencies and to have a consistent environment for e.g. screenshots/visual regression testing across different operating systems.
llm_response:
The CI runner is missing the necessary operating system dependencies required to launch the browsers. While your local machines have these libraries pre-installed, the `ubuntu-latest` runner requires them to be explicitly installed.

The durable way to fix this is to use the command `npx playwright install --with-deps` in your GitHub Actions workflow. This command installs both the browsers and all required operating system dependencies.

In your `.github/workflows/playwright.yml` file, ensure you have the following step included:

```yaml
- name: Install Playwright Browsers
  run: npx playwright install --with-deps
```

Alternatively, if you prefer to use a containerized environment to ensure a consistent environment that includes all necessary dependencies, you can use the official Playwright Docker image in your workflow:

```yaml
jobs:
  playwright:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    container:
      image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.60.0-noble
```

Using `npx playwright install --with-deps` is the standard approach for non-containerized GitHub Actions runners.

user_input: Almost all of our tests stub the search endpoint so they're hermetic, and that's been great until the backend quietly renamed a field and every test stayed green while production broke. I want to keep most tests stubbed but have a couple that exercise the real endpoint and only override one flag in whatever comes back. Can the same interception mechanism do both, and what changes between them?
reference: Both go through the same route handler; what differs is whether you ever let the request reach the network. A hermetic stub never does: page.route(url, route => route.fulfill({ json: ... })) answers from the test and the server is never contacted, which is why a server-side shape change can't fail it. To modify a real response you have to fetch it first — inside the handler call `const response = await route.fetch()`, read the real body with `await response.json()`, mutate the field you care about, and then fulfill with the edited payload: `await route.fulfill({ response, json })`. That gives you the real contract for everything you didn't touch, so the renamed field would have surfaced. Routes are matched most-recently-registered first and are scoped to the page or context they were registered on, so a spec-level `page.route` override can sit on top of a project-wide stub. If you want the real traffic recorded once and replayed thereafter, that's what HAR replay is for.
reference_contexts: Mock API requests: All the requests made by the page, including XHRs and fetch requests, can be tracked, modified and mocked.
await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => { const json = [{ name: 'Strawberry', id: 21 }]; await route.fulfill({ json }); });

await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => { const response = await route.fetch(); const json = await response.json(); json.push({ name: 'Loquat', id: 100 }); // Fulfill using the original response, while patching the response body with the given JSON object. await route.fulfill({ response, json }); });
llm_response:
Yes, the same interception mechanism can be used for both stubbing and exercising the real endpoint with modifications. You can use `page.route` to intercept requests and `route.fallback` to handle the logic.

When multiple routes match a pattern, they run in the order opposite to their registration. To achieve your goal, you can register a handler that performs the modification and then calls `route.fallback()` to allow the request to proceed to the real backend.

**How it works:**
*   **For stubbing:** You define a route handler that fulfills the request with your stubbed data (without calling `route.fallback()`).
*   **For exercising the real endpoint with an override:** You register a handler that fetches the real response (or allows it to proceed) and then modifies the data. By using `route.fallback()`, you ensure that other matching handlers are invoked. 

As described in the documentation, the last registered route can override previous ones. You can structure your tests so that the specific test requiring the real endpoint registers its handler last, ensuring it takes precedence or interacts with the existing handlers via `route.fallback()`.

Added in: v1.23

route.fallback

Continues route's request with optional overrides. The method is similar to
route.continue() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-route#route-continue)

Usage

When several routes match the given pattern, they run in the order opposite to their registration. That way the last registered route can always override all the previous ones. In the example below, request will be handled by the bottom-most handler first, then it'll fall back to the previous one and in the end will be aborted by the first registered route.

user_input: How does device emulation (viewport, user agent, touch) get applied per test, and why doesn't it bleed into other tests?
reference: Device parameters come from Playwright's device registry and are applied at the browser-context level. Since every test runs in its own isolated context — which can also carry mobile emulation, permissions, locale and color scheme — the emulation stays scoped to that test.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

Browser contexts can also be used to emulate multi-page scenarios involving mobile devices, permissions, locale and color scheme. Check out our Emulation (https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation) guide for more details.
llm_response:
Device emulation is applied per test or per test group by configuring the `use` option within a `test.describe` block or a `test` file. Alternatively, it can be applied globally or per project in the `playwright.config.ts` file. When using the library directly, emulation is applied by passing device parameters into `browser.newContext()`.

Emulation does not bleed into other tests because Playwright creates a new browser context for each test. By using `test.use()` within a specific block or by defining separate projects in the configuration, the emulation settings are scoped to those specific tests or contexts. When using the library directly, the settings are applied only to the specific context created with those parameters.

Some tests now fail with a message about the test itself rather than the assertion, and raising the assertion timeout further doesn't help those at all. How many separate budgets am I actually dealing with, and which one do I raise?
reference: Three budgets, nested, which is why raising the wrong one does nothing. The test timeout is 30 seconds by default and covers the whole test — the test function plus fixture setup plus beforeEach hooks — and it's what you're hitting when the failure names the test rather than an assertion; raise it in the config's `timeout`, or per test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or test.slow() to triple the default. Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own separate 5-second expect timeout, which is unrelated to the test timeout and is the one reported in a 'expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms' call log; set it globally with `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` or per assertion with a { timeout } option. Because the assertion budget is consumed inside the test budget, pushing the expect timeout above the test timeout accomplishes nothing — the test dies first. beforeAll/afterAll get their own timeout, equal to the test timeout by default and adjustable inside the hook. The right fix for a uniformly slower machine is the config-level defaults, not per-assertion overrides.

export default defineConfig({ expect: { timeout: 10_000, }, });
test('very slow test', async ({ page }) => { test.setTimeout(120_000); }); test.slow(); // Easy way to triple the default timeout

llm_response:
You are dealing with three separate budgets:

1.  **Assertion timeout:** This is for a single assertion, which you have been adjusting using the `timeout` option in `expect` (e.g., `await expect(locator).toHaveText('hello', { timeout: 10_000 });`) [7].
2.  **Test timeout:** This governs the duration of the test itself. When you see errors about the test failing rather than the assertion, you have likely hit this limit. You can configure this per file or per describe block using `test.describe.configure({ timeout: 20_000 })` [3].
3.  **Global timeout:** This is the maximum time allowed for the entire test suite to run. You can set this in your `playwright.config.ts` file using the `globalTimeout` property [7].

Since your tests are failing with messages about the test itself rather than the assertion, you should raise the **test timeout** using `test.describe.configure`.

#### Fail-Fast​ {#fail-fast}

Large test suites can take very long to execute. By executing a preliminary test run with the
`--only-changed`
flag, you can run test files that are likely to fail first. This will give you a faster feedback loop and slightly lower CI consumption while working on Pull Requests. To detect test files affected by your changeset,
`--only-changed`

## Shard tests between multiple machines​ {#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines}

Playwright Test can shard a test suite, so that it can be executed on multiple machines. See

## Limit failures and fail fast​ {#limit-failures-and-fail-fast}

You can limit the number of failed tests in the whole test suite by setting
`maxFailures`
config option or passing
`--max-failures`
command line flag.

When running with "max failures" set, Playwright Test will stop after reaching this number of failed tests and skip any tests that were not executed yet. This is useful to avoid wasting resources on broken test suites.

Passing command line option:


`npx playwrighttest--max-failures=10`

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

## Sharding tests between multiple machines​ {#sharding-tests-between-multiple-machines}

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:


`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`


Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

<https://playwright.dev/docs/pom>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Large test suites can be structured to optimize ease of authoring and maintenance. Page object models are one such approach to structure your test suite.

user_input: Before a click, what does Playwright verify, and how does that relate to the waiting a plain click already does?
reference: A click runs actionability checks — attached, visible, stable, receives pointer events, enabled — and auto-waits for them. The pointer methods bake that same sequence in (down to scrolling into view), so you rarely need explicit waits.
reference_contexts: Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given timeout , action fails with the TimeoutError .
wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
llm_response:
Before performing a `locator.click()`, Playwright performs a range of actionability checks to ensure the action behaves as expected. Specifically, it verifies that:

*   The locator resolves to exactly one element.
*   The element is visible.
*   The element is stable (not animating or has completed animation).
*   The element receives events (is not obscured by other elements).
*   The element is enabled.

These checks are part of Playwright's "auto-waiting" mechanism. Playwright automatically waits for all these relevant checks to pass before performing the click. If these checks do not pass within the specified `timeout`, the action fails with a `TimeoutError`. 

This auto-waiting behavior can be bypassed by using the `force` option, which disables non-essential actionability checks.
llm_references:
Playwright also includes generic matchers like
`toEqual`
,
`toContain`
,
`toBeTruthy`
that can be used to assert any conditions. These assertions do not use the
`await`
keyword as they perform immediate synchronous checks on already available values.


`expect(success).toBeTruthy();`

Playwright Test is based on the concept of
test fixtures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures)
such as the
built in page fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#built-in-fixtures)
, which is passed into your test. Pages are
isolated between tests due to the Browser Context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
, which is equivalent to a brand new browser profile. Every test gets a fresh environment, even when multiple tests run in a single browser.

<https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given
`timeout`
, action fails with the
`TimeoutError`
.

For example, for
locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click)
, Playwright will ensure that:

locator resolves to exactly one element
element is

element is
Stable (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#stable)
, as in not animating or completed animation
element
Receives Events (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#receives-events)
, as in not obscured by other elements
element is
Enabled (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability#enabled)

Waits for the matching request and returns it. See

reference: Downloaded files sit in a temporary folder and belong to whichever context fetched them, so they vanish the instant that context is torn down. Each test gets a freshly created context, so grab anything you need before the test ends.
reference_contexts: Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.

Downloaded files are stored in a temporary directory by default. You can specify a custom directory for downloads using the `downloadsPath` option in `browserType.launch()` or the `artifactsDir` option (which is not cleaned up when the browser closes).

Files may disappear before you can use them for the following reasons:

*   **Browser Context Closure:** Downloaded files are automatically deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
*   **Temporary Directory Cleanup:** If you do not specify a persistent directory (like `artifactsDir`), the temporary directory used for downloads is cleaned up when the browser closes.
*   **Control Flow Issues:** If you handle the download event without awaiting the operation, your script might finish and close the browser context while the download is still in progress.
*   **Manual Deletion:** The `download.delete()` method can be used to explicitly delete a downloaded file.

To ensure you can use the files, you should use `await download.saveAs(path)` to copy the download to a user-specified path.

It's unusable — it fails on the first run of any new test, it fails constantly on CI with what look like anti-aliasing differences, and there's no way to accept a legitimate design change short of regenerating files by hand. reference: Each of your three problems is a thing the built-in assertion already handles, because capturing an image and asserting on one are different operations. page.screenshot() just returns a buffer; expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() is a full comparison assertion. On first run there is no baseline, so instead of failing meaninglessly it takes screenshots until two consecutive ones match — which also settles animation and rendering noise — saves the result as the reference and reports that it wrote it; you commit that file. On CI, the baseline is keyed by environment: the snapshot name like example-test-1-chromium-darwin.png encodes the browser and platform (the project name replaces the browser when you use multiple projects) precisely because rendering, fonts and anti-aliasing differ across platforms, so Linux CI compares against its own baseline rather than your macOS one. And byte-exactness isn't required: `maxDiffPixels` (per assertion or globally under `expect: { toHaveScreenshot: ... }`) sets an allowance. When a change is intentional you re-baseline with `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` rather than editing files.

The built-in comparison handles your three points as follows:

*   **Failing on the first run:** Playwright snapshot testing is designed to capture the state at a given moment to be saved for future comparisons [3]. When a snapshot does not yet exist, the test runner handles the initial creation of the reference file.
*   **Failing on anti-aliasing/minor differences:** Unlike a byte-for-byte comparison, Playwright uses the `pixelmatch` library [7], which allows for configurable tolerance. You can use the `threshold` option to set an acceptable perceived color difference in the YIQ color space (defaulting to 0.2) [2, 5], or the `maxDiffPixels` option to allow a specific number of pixels to differ [1, 5, 7].
*   **Accepting legitimate design changes:** You do not need to regenerate files by hand. You can update snapshots automatically by running the command `npx playwright test --update-snapshots` [7].

### Snapshot testing​ {#snapshot-testing}

Snapshot testing captures a “snapshot” or representation of the entire state of an element, component, or data at a given moment, which is then saved for future comparisons. When re-running tests, the current state is compared to the snapshot, and if there are differences, the test fails. This approach is especially useful for complex or dynamic structures, where manually asserting each detail would be too time-consuming. Snapshot testing is broader and more holistic than assertion testing, allowing you to track more complex changes over time.

Advantages

Simplifies complex outputs
: For example, testing a UI component's rendered output can be tedious with traditional assertions. Snapshots capture the entire output for easy comparison.
Quick Feedback loop
: Developers can easily spot unintended changes in the output.
Encourages consistency
: Helps maintain consistent output as code evolves.

Disadvantages

If the tree structure matches the template, the test passes; otherwise, it fails, indicating a mismatch between expected and actual accessibility states.
The comparison is case-sensitive and collapses whitespace, so indentation and line breaks are ignored.
The comparison is order-sensitive, meaning the order of elements in the snapshot template must match the order in the page's accessibility tree.

### Partial matching​ {#partial-matching}

You can perform partial matches on nodes by omitting attributes or accessible names, enabling verification of specific parts of the accessibility tree without requiring exact matches. This flexibility is helpful for dynamic or irrelevant attributes.

An automated scan — the documented approach uses the @axe-core/playwright package, where you await `new AxeBuilder({ page }).analyze()` and assert the returned `violations` array is empty — detects *rule* violations such as missing or invalid properties. It has no opinion about whether the structure is the one you intended, and the docs are explicit that many accessibility problems can only be found through manual testing, recommending a combination of automated scans, manual assessment and inclusive user testing. What your refactor changed was the shape of the accessibility tree, and that is what an aria snapshot pins: expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot() captures a YAML representation of the accessibility tree — the hierarchy of accessible elements with their roles, attributes, values and text, with indentation carrying the nesting — and fails when the current tree stops matching it. Order and nesting are part of that representation, so a moved section shows as a diff. The two compose: accessibility tests are ordinary tests, so you can put both in one spec or keep separate ones. Bear in mind the tradeoff the docs draw between the styles — targeted assertions check one specific condition and get verbose over complex structures, while snapshots capture whole-structure state and are best for outputs that rarely change shape, which also means they need deliberate re-baselining when a change is intentional.
reference_contexts: The following examples rely on the @axe-core/playwright package which adds support for running the axe accessibility testing engine as part of your Playwright tests.

Automated accessibility tests can detect some common accessibility problems such as missing or invalid properties. But many accessibility problems can only be discovered through manual testing. We recommend using a combination of automated testing, manual accessibility assessments, and inclusive user testing.
Accessibility tests work just like any other Playwright test. You can either create separate test cases for them, or integrate accessibility scans and assertions into your existing test cases.

In Playwright, aria snapshots provide a YAML representation of the accessibility tree of a page. These snapshots can be stored and compared later to verify if the page structure remains consistent or meets defined expectations.

The YAML format describes the hierarchical structure of accessible elements on the page, detailing roles, attributes, values, and text content. The structure follows a tree-like syntax, where each node represents an accessible element, and indentation indicates nested elements.
Snapshot testing is ideal for: UI testing of whole pages and components. Broad structural checks for complex UI components. Regression testing for outputs that rarely change structure.

## Handling known issues​ {#handling-known-issues}

A common question when adding accessibility tests to an application is "how do I suppress known violations?" The following examples demonstrate a few techniques you can use.

### Excluding individual elements from a scan​ {#excluding-individual-elements-from-a-scan}

Here is an example of excluding one element from being scanned in one specific test:


`test('should not have any accessibility violations outside of elements with known issues',async({page,})=>{awaitpage.goto('https://your-site.com/page-with-known-issues');constaccessibilityScanResults=awaitnewAxeBuilder({page}).exclude('#element-with-known-issue').analyze();expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);});`


If the element in question is used repeatedly in many pages, consider
using a test fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/accessibility-testing#using-a-test-fixture-for-common-axe-configuration)
to reuse the same
`AxeBuilder`
configuration across multiple tests.

### Disabling individual scan rules​ {#disabling-individual-scan-rules}

`test('navigation menu should not have automatically detectable accessibility violations',async({page,})=>{awaitpage.goto('https://your-site.com/');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Navigation Menu'}).click();// It is important to waitFor() the page to be in the desired// state *before* running analyze(). Otherwise, axe might not// find all the elements your test expects it to scan.awaitpage.locator('#navigation-menu-flyout').waitFor();constaccessibilityScanResults=awaitnewAxeBuilder({page}).include('#navigation-menu-flyout').analyze();expect(accessibilityScanResults.violations).toEqual([]);});`


### Scanning for WCAG violations​ {#scanning-for-wcag-violations}

By default, axe checks against a wide variety of accessibility rules. Some of these rules correspond to specific success criteria from the
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) (https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/)
, and others are "best practice" rules that are not specifically required by any WCAG criterion.

Test fixtures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures)

user_input: I need to assert that every row in our pricing table renders right-aligned, which isn't in the DOM anywhere — it's a computed style. Nothing on the locator exposes it, and my first attempt at reaching into the page came back with undefined for the threshold I was comparing against, even though it's a plain number defined right above the call.
reference: Two boundaries are in play. First, to get at computed style you have to run code in the page: a locator resolves to elements but only exposes what the API models, so anything the API doesn't cover you obtain with evaluate. For the whole set at once use locator.evaluateAll(), whose callback receives the array of matching elements — e.g. `await page.locator('td.price').evaluateAll(els => els.map(e => getComputedStyle(e).textAlign))` — returning an ordinary array back into the test. Second, that callback executes in the browser, in a different context from your test file, so it cannot close over test variables; that's why your threshold was undefined rather than throwing at definition. Pass it explicitly as the second argument: `locator.evaluateAll((els, limit) => ..., limit)`. Whatever you return has to be serializable to cross back — return the strings or numbers you want to assert on, not DOM nodes.
reference_contexts: The code inside locator.evaluateAll() runs in the page, you can call any DOM apis there.
const rows = page.getByRole('listitem'); const texts = await rows.evaluateAll( list => list.map(element => element.textContent));

Evaluated scripts run in the browser environment, while your test runs in a testing environments. This means you cannot use variables from your test in the page and vice versa. Instead, you should pass them explicitly as an argument.

user_input: I want to parameterize the same tests with different values — both at the test level and across environments. How do these two levels differ?
reference: You can parameterize at the test level or the project level. Project-level parameterization uses option fixtures whose values you set in each project's config, which is how you run the same tests against different environments.
reference_contexts: You can either parameterize tests on a test level or on a project level.

Playwright Test supports running multiple test projects that can be configured separately. You can use "option" fixtures to make your configuration options declarative and type safe. Learn more about parameterizing tests (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parameterize) .
llm_response:
The difference between parameterizing tests at the test level and across environments (project level) is as follows:

**Test Level Parameterization**
*   **Mechanism:** You use a `forEach` loop within your test file to iterate over an array of data. You can apply this to individual `test()` calls or wrap them in `test.describe()` blocks.
*   **Usage:** This is used to run the same test logic multiple times with different input values (e.g., different names and expected results).
*   **Hooks:** You can place `beforeEach`, `beforeAll`, `afterEach`, and `afterAll` hooks outside the `forEach` loop to execute them once, or inside a `test.describe()` block within the loop to execute them for each iteration.

**Environment/Project Level Parameterization**
*   **Mechanism:** You define multiple projects within the `playwright.config.ts` file using the `projects` array.
*   **Usage:** This is used to run a group of tests against different environments (e.g., staging vs. production) or with different configurations, such as varying timeouts or retry counts.
*   **Environment Differentiation:** To differentiate environments when running the same tests across multiple machines, you can use the `testConfig.tag` property in your configuration file to tag tests with the environment name.
*   **Environment Variables:** You can also configure tests using environment variables passed from the command line, which can be accessed within your tests via `process.env` or read directly in the `playwright.config.ts` file.

One spec in our checkout suite never finishes — the runner sits on it until the whole run is killed. It's the test that exercises the 'delete saved card' button, which is the only place in the app that asks the user to confirm before proceeding. I added a listener so I could log what the prompt says, and the message does get printed, so it's not that we're missing the event. reference: The dialog listener must actually handle the dialog by calling dialog.accept() or dialog.dismiss(); otherwise the action stalls because dialogs are modals that block page execution. Fix by accepting/dismissing, e.g. page.on('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept()).
reference_contexts: page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) listener must handle the dialog. Otherwise your action will stall, be it locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click) or something else. That's because dialogs in Web are modals and therefore block further page execution until they are handled.

page.on('dialog', dialog => console.log(dialog.message()));

llm_response:
Your test is hanging because you are not handling the dialog. When a JavaScript dialog (such as `confirm`) appears, the page freezes and waits for the dialog to be either accepted or dismissed. If you use a `page.on('dialog', ...)` listener, you **must** call either `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()` within that listener.

Your current code only logs the message, which causes the action (the click) to stall indefinitely.

To fix this, update your listener to accept the dialog:

```javascript
page.on('dialog', dialog => dialog.accept());
await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete card' }).click();
```

If you do not provide a listener at all, Playwright will automatically dismiss the dialog, which would also allow your click action to complete.

The test is not wrong, and CI is not wrong. The error message indicates that there is no "golden file" (reference snapshot) yet.

When you run `await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` for the first time, the test runner generates the actual screenshot but fails because it has no existing reference to compare it against. It saves the actual screenshot to the file system so that it can be added to the repository.

Because snapshots include the browser name and platform (e.g., `chromium-darwin`) in their filename, they differ between environments. If your local environment and CI environment differ in platform or browser rendering, the snapshot generated locally will not match what is expected in CI.

To resolve this:
1. You must commit the generated snapshot directory (e.g., `example.spec.ts-snapshots`) to your version control system.
2. If the snapshot was generated in an environment that does not match your CI environment, you may need to update the snapshots using the `--update-snapshots` command line flag to ensure the reference files match the expected output for your CI environment.

### Snapshot testing​ {#snapshot-testing}

Snapshot testing captures a “snapshot” or representation of the entire state of an element, component, or data at a given moment, which is then saved for future comparisons. When re-running tests, the current state is compared to the snapshot, and if there are differences, the test fails. This approach is especially useful for complex or dynamic structures, where manually asserting each detail would be too time-consuming. Snapshot testing is broader and more holistic than assertion testing, allowing you to track more complex changes over time.

Advantages

Simplifies complex outputs
: For example, testing a UI component's rendered output can be tedious with traditional assertions. Snapshots capture the entire output for easy comparison.
Quick Feedback loop
: Developers can easily spot unintended changes in the output.
Encourages consistency
: Helps maintain consistent output as code evolves.

Disadvantages

reference: :has-text() matches any element containing the text, so used alone it matches many elements including <body>. Combine it with another CSS specifier, e.g. await page.locator('article:has-text("Playwright")').click();
reference_contexts: Note that :has-text() should be used together with other CSS specifiers, otherwise it will match all the elements containing specified text, including the <body> .
llm_response:
The `:has-text("Playwright")` selector matches the `<body>` element because the text "Playwright" exists somewhere within the body, and the selector finds every element that contains that text.

To narrow this to the specific element you want, you should use a more precise locator that uniquely identifies the target:

*   **Recommended approach:** Use a locator that specifies the container or the element type, such as `page.locator('article:has-text("Playwright")')`. This restricts the search to only the `<article>` element containing the text.
*   **Alternative approach:** Use `page.getByRole()` to locate the element based on how users and assistive technology perceive it (e.g., `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Playwright' })`). This is generally preferred for pinpointing exact elements.

Avoid using `locator.first()`, `locator.last()`, or `locator.nth()` to resolve multiple matches, as these are not recommended; if the page structure changes, Playwright may click on an unintended element.

reference: Mock Service Worker registers a service worker that grabs the traffic first, so Playwright's route() never sees it. Either set serviceWorkers to 'block' to remove that layer, or drop MSW and mock responses with Playwright's own routing.
reference_contexts: It might be that you are using a mock tool such as Mock Service Worker (MSW). While this tool works out of the box for mocking responses, it adds its own Service Worker that takes over the network requests, hence making them invisible to browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) .

If you're using Playwright's native browserContext.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-route) and page.route() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-route) , and it appears network events are missing, disable Service Workers by setting serviceWorkers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browser#browser-new-context-option-service-workers) to 'block' .
llm_response:
The MSW Service Worker is taking over the network requests, making them invisible to `page.route()`.

To resolve this, you have two options:

## Worker index and parallel index​ {#worker-index-and-parallel-index}

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between
`0`
and
`workers - 1`
. When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same
`parallelIndex`
and a new
`workerIndex`
.

You can read an index from environment variables
`process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX`
and
`process.env.TEST_PARALLEL_INDEX`

testInfo.workerIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-worker-index)
and
testInfo.parallelIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-parallel-index)
.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

My click fails because a hover overlay intercepts the click at the action point, even though I know the element is fine. Code:

await page.getByRole('button').click(); // fails actionability / receives-events

How can I bypass the check?
reference: Actionability checks include the element receiving pointer events; an overlay intercepting the click causes failure. If you know this is happening, bypass the checks with force: true, e.g. await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true }).
reference_contexts: Sometimes, apps use non-trivial logic where hovering the element overlays it with another element that intercepts the click. This behavior is indistinguishable from a bug where element gets covered and the click is dispatched elsewhere. If you know this is taking place, you can bypass the actionability (https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability) checks and force the click:
await page.getByRole('button').click({ force: true });

Some actions like locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click) support force option that disables non-essential actionability checks, for example passing truthy force to locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click) method will not check that the target element actually receives click events.
llm_response:
To bypass the actionability checks when a hover overlay intercepts your click, you can use the `force` option. This disables non-essential actionability checks, such as the requirement that the element must be non-obscured by other elements to receive pointer events.

You can implement this as follows:

```javascript
await page.getByRole('button').click({force: true});
```

Alternatively, if you want to simulate the click by dispatching a click event directly on the element, you can use:

```javascript
await page.getByRole('button').dispatchEvent('click');
```

## Modify API responses​ {#modify-api-responses}

Sometimes, it is essential to make an API request, but the response needs to be patched to allow for reproducible testing. In that case, instead of mocking the request, one can perform the request and fulfill it with the modified response.

In the example below we intercept the call to the fruit API and add a new fruit called 'Loquat', to the data. We then go to the url and assert that this data is there:


`test('gets the json from api and adds a new fruit',async({page})=>{// Get the response and add to itawaitpage.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits',asyncroute=>{constresponse=awaitroute.fetch();constjson=awaitresponse.json();json.push({name:'Loquat',id:100});// Fulfill using the original response, while patching the response body// with the given JSON object.awaitroute.fulfill({response,json});});// Go to the pageawaitpage.goto('https://demo.playwright.dev/api-mocking');// Assert that the new fruit is visibleawaitexpect(page.getByText('Loquat',{exact:true})).toBeVisible();});`


In the trace of our test we can see that the API was called and the response was modified.

By inspecting the response we can see that our new fruit was added to the list.

llm_response:
To see exactly what happened when a test fails on CI without slowing down the whole run, you should enable `trace: 'on-first-retry'` in your test configuration file. This will produce a `trace.zip` file for each test that was retried, allowing you to use the Trace Viewer to inspect actions, logs, and DOM snapshots.

If you are not using retries but still want traces for failed tests, you can use `trace: 'retain-on-failure'` instead.

user_input: Our dashboard greets people with 'Good morning' or 'Good evening' and stamps every row with a relative label like 'posted 3 hours ago'. The assertions on both pass when I run them at my desk and fail on the nightly build, which is obviously about when the run happens rather than the code. How do I make the page's idea of the current time deterministic?
reference: Pin the clock rather than trying to write assertions that hold at any hour. The recommended tool is page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00')), which fixes what Date.now() and new Date() return so the greeting and the relative timestamps render the same way on every run. You can call it again mid-test to move to another fixed instant and re-assert. Reach for clock.install() only if the page's timers actually need time to progress — install is the heavier option that additionally lets you pauseAt, fastForward, runFor and resume — and setSystemTime is for advanced cases only.
reference_contexts: setFixedTime: Sets the fixed time for Date.now() and new Date().

The recommended approach is to use setFixedTime to set the time to a specific value. If that doesn't work for your use case, you can use install which allows you to pause time later on, fast forward it, tick it, etc. setSystemTime is only recommended for advanced use cases.
await page.clock.setFixedTime(new Date('2024-02-02T10:00:00')); await page.goto('http://localhost:3333'); await expect(page.getByTestId('current-time')).toHaveText('2/2/2024, 10:00:00 AM');
llm_response:
To make the page's time deterministic, you should use `page.clock` to control the time. You must call `await page.clock.install()` before any other clock-related calls to avoid undefined behavior.

Depending on your specific needs, you can use the following approaches:

*   **To set a fixed time while keeping timers running:** Use `await page.clock.setFixedTime(time)`. This allows time to flow naturally while `Date.now()` returns a fixed value.
*   **To have manual control over time flow:**
    1.  Initialize the clock: `await page.clock.install({ time: new Date('...') })`.
    2.  Pause the time flow: `await page.clock.pauseAt(new Date('...'))`.
    3.  Advance time as needed:
        *   Use `await page.clock.fastForward('duration')` to jump forward by a specific duration (e.g., `'30:00'`).
        *   Use `await page.clock.runFor(milliseconds)` to tick forward manually and fire timers.
*   **To test time shifts without triggering timers:** Use `await page.clock.setSystemTime(time)`. This is intended for testing scenarios like time zone changes or daylight savings transitions.

# Web server | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-webserver>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright comes with a
`webServer`
option in the config file which gives you the ability to launch a local dev server before running your tests. This is ideal for when writing your tests during development and when you don't have a staging or production url to test against.

## Configuring a web server​ {#configuring-a-web-server}

Use the
`webServer`
property in your Playwright config to launch a development web server during the tests.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Run your local dev server before starting the testswebServer:{command:'npm run start',url:'http://localhost:3000',reuseExistingServer:!process.env.CI,stdout:'ignore',stderr:'pipe',},});`

### Using on CI​ {#using-on-ci}

See our
Continuous Integration guides (https://playwright.dev/docs/ci)
for sample configs.

### Remote Connection​ {#remote-connection}

You can run Playwright Server in Docker while keeping your tests running on the host system or another machine. This is useful for running tests on unsupported Linux distributions or remote execution scenarios.

#### Running the Playwright Server​ {#running-the-playwright-server}

Start the Playwright Server in Docker:


`dockerrun-p3000:3000--rm--init-it--workdir/home/pwuser--userpwuser mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.60.0-noble /bin/sh-c"npx -y playwright@1.60.0 run-server --port 3000 --host 0.0.0.0"`


#### Connecting to the Server​ {#connecting-to-the-server}

There are two ways to connect to the remote Playwright server:

Using environment variable with
`@playwright/test`
:


`PW_TEST_CONNECT_WS_ENDPOINT=ws://127.0.0.1:3000/ npx playwrighttest`

`# Install NPM packagesnpmci# Install Playwright browsers and dependenciesnpx playwrightinstall--with-deps`

Run your tests
:

`npx playwrighttest`


## Workers​ {#workers}

We recommend setting
workers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-workers)
to "1" in CI environments to prioritize stability and reproducibility. Running tests sequentially ensures each test gets the full system resources, avoiding potential conflicts. However, if you have a powerful self-hosted CI system, you may enable
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
tests. For wider parallelization, consider
sharding (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#shard-tests-between-multiple-machines)
- distributing tests across multiple CI jobs.

playwright.config.ts

`import{defineConfig,devices}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Opt out of parallel tests on CI.workers:process.env.CI?1:undefined,});`


## CI configurations​ {#ci-configurations}

Details

If the port is specified, Playwright Test will wait for it to be available on
`127.0.0.1`
or
`::1`
, before running the tests. If the url is specified, Playwright Test will wait for the URL to return a 2xx, 3xx, 400, 401, 402, or 403 status code before running the tests.

For continuous integration, you may want to use the
`reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI`
option which does not use an existing server on the CI. To see the stdout, you can set the

environment variable.

The
`port`

`url`

testOptions.baseURL (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-base-url)

`8080`
produces

equal
`http://localhost:8080`

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Test retries are a way to automatically re-run a test when it fails. This is useful when a test is flaky and fails intermittently. Test retries are configured in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)

## Failures​ {#failures}

The recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state is to use one account per parallel worker. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once, and all tests run by that worker reuse the same authentication state.

To implement this, you should:

1.  **Create a worker-scoped fixture:** Create a `playwright/fixtures.ts` file to define an account fixture. You must use the `{scope: 'worker'}` option so the test runner sets the fixture up once per worker.
2.  **Differentiate workers:** Use `workerInfo.workerIndex` (or `testInfo.workerIndex` / `testInfo.parallelIndex` as referenced in specific implementation contexts) to generate or select a unique account for each worker process.
3.  **Override or initialize:** Depending on your needs, you can either override the `storageState` fixture to authenticate once per worker or create a custom fixture (e.g., `dbUserName`) to initialize a new user in the test database for that specific worker.

# Parallelism | Playwright

<https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel>

## Introduction​ {#introduction}

Playwright Test runs tests in parallel. In order to achieve that, it runs several worker processes that run at the same time. By default,
test files
are run in parallel. Tests in a single file are run in order, in the same worker process.

You can configure tests using
test.describe.configure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#parallelize-tests-in-a-single-file)
to run
tests in a single file
in parallel.
You can configure
entire project
to have all tests in all files to run in parallel using
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
or
testConfig.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-fully-parallel)
.
To
disable
parallelism limit the number of
workers to one (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#disable-parallelism)
.

You can control the number of
parallel worker processes (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-workers)
and
limit the number of failures (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#limit-failures-and-fail-fast)
in the whole test suite for efficiency.

## Worker processes​ {#worker-processes}

All tests run in worker processes. These processes are OS processes, running independently, orchestrated by the test runner. All workers have identical environments and each starts its own browser.

You can't communicate between the workers. Playwright Test reuses a single worker as much as it can to make testing faster, so multiple test files are usually run in a single worker one after another.

Workers are always shutdown after a
test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures)
to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.

reference: Prefer user-facing locators like role and text (getByRole, getByText) or an explicit test id contract (getByTestId) instead of CSS/XPath, which are tied to implementation and break when the DOM changes.
reference_contexts: CSS and XPath are not recommended as the DOM can often change leading to non resilient tests. Instead, try to come up with a locator that is close to how the user perceives the page such as role locators or define an explicit testing contract using test ids.
